source.title: Scaling recipes for single-cell RNA sequencing foundation models: when do scaling laws hold?
source.authors: Federico Borra; Giacomo Cirò; Arianna Castellini; G. Gatti; A. Tangherloni; Francesca M. Buffa

record.file_problem: Full, readable paper text is present. Some figure layout is flattened, but the main text and methods are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in transcriptomic models and finds it differs substantially by model formulation and context length; it argues scaling relationships are empirical and setting-specific rather than universally transferable.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own pre-training-loss scaling results, held-out largest-model targets, loss-surface validation, and downstream BIOscore trends. The loss-surface results use a quadratic response surface, not a power law. Learning-rate scaling results are not rows for the claim versions because they measure an optimization hyperparameter rather than the claimed loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: The study trains transcriptomic transformer encoders in a new, non-text setting. It fits L ∝ N^-k to its own pre-training losses across context lengths and two formulations, and checks downstream BIOscore against pre-training progress. This bears on V5 (power-law form beyond text), V7 (exponents depend on setup) and V6 (downstream tracks loss). It is not a language-model study, and the extrapolation it attempts spans only about a factor of 5 with no stated accuracy, so V1–V4 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. Two additions: the authors also state that some scaling coefficients differ in magnitude from LM values, with one sign reversed (the learning-rate depth exponent). They also say the fitted relationships give no guarantee beyond the examined range.
record.recipe_differences: Transcriptomic transformer encoders trained on masked gene identity or binned expression, rather than language-model next-token prediction. The study varies context, model size, compute, and architecture and fits local scaling relationships.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling regularity and fitted coefficients vary with formulation and context length. Downstream BIOscore is affected by embedding width because wider embeddings give the linear probe greater expressive power.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal learning rate follows a power law in N, with |αN| from 0.26 to 0.57, larger than about 0.14 for LMs. For Ranked, the depth exponent is positive, the reverse of the LM direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal-hyperparameter scaling exponents transfer across domains.

fits_no_version.finding: A quadratic surface in N, C and depth-to-width ratio predicts held-out loss well for Ranked (R²≈0.98) and worse for Binned (R²≈0.87). The Binned shape optimum is unstable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-variable loss surfaces interpolate loss and yield compute-optimal shape.

record.code_released: not stated; authors say code will be made available as a GitHub repository upon publication.
record.peer_reviewed: bioRxiv preprint; not certified by peer review
record.problems: Each architecture was trained once, with no independent training-seed replicates. The test partition was reserved but not used. Initial size-law fits compare configurations at approximately fixed steps and examples, not fixed compute; the largest model is a held-out target, but its prediction accuracy is not numerically described in the text. The Binned Gene Expression response-surface optima are highly unstable; about 15% of bootstrap surfaces are non-convex. Downstream findings are described as indicative, and wider models have an evaluation advantage from greater probe expressivity. The authors note that compute estimates exclude data loading, optimizer updates, and device-utilization overhead.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows omitted. Learning-rate scaling and depth-to-width optima were not catalogued as results for V1–V7: they concern optimal learning rate or architectural shape, not the claimed parameter/token compute-optimal allocation or held-out loss law.

untested.parts: Language models are not studied. Loss is fitted only against non-embedding parameters at a fixed step, not against tokens or compute.
A largest-model held-out target exists, but it is only about 5x beyond the fit range and its prediction error is not quantified in the text. There is no orders-of-magnitude extrapolation.
There is no parameter-versus-token compute-optimal split; only the optimal depth-to-width ratio is estimated.
Depth and width are varied, but the loss sensitivity to shape at fixed N is not reported as a quantity.
Only static scRNA-seq encoders are studied. There are no image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer, and no scaling in data or compute.
Parameter counting, schedule and fitting-method choices are not varied for the loss law.

missing.what: Held-out largest-model predicted versus observed loss gaps, per context and formulation
Binned per-context k values (about -0.007 to 0.016, including one negative)
Loss versus cumulative compute curves for 1M–1B models; no power-law fit is stated

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3: this is a new-domain test with positive results for one formulation, not an argument that a version is wrong. The size sweep compares runs at a fixed step rather than fixed compute, and each architecture was trained once. V2 is not credited because the extrapolation is small and unquantified.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines transcriptomic models, not language models, and does not test the stated language-model loss law across parameters, tokens, and compute.

It tests largest-model prediction from smaller-model power-law fits only in its transcriptomic setting; it does not test language-model runs or orders-of-magnitude extrapolation beyond the studied ranges.
The study estimates an optimal depth-to-width ratio, not the loss-minimizing parameter-count/token-count split as a function of compute.
The study varies depth and width but does not establish whether loss changes only slightly across a wide range of architectural details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests static single-cell transcriptomic models. It does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream assessment is limited to the study’s BIOscore and its components on the tested transcriptomic models and validation data.

It shows dependence on model formulation and context length, but does not compare language-model fitting choices such as token/parameter accounting or training schedules, nor establish that curves bend away from power laws in language models.

relationships.condition: Ranked Gene Identity, contexts 128–2048, 396K–42.5M non-embedding params
relationships.reason: Cross-entropy falls roughly linearly on log-log axes at every context, with k from 0.022 to 0.092 (r1–r5).
relationships.display_finding: Cross-entropy decreased approximately linearly on log-log axes at every context length, with k=0.022–0.092.

relationships.reason: MSE scaling is weak and irregular: k is about 0.01, one fitted k is negative, and there is no monotone trend with context (r6–r10).
relationships.display_finding: MSE scaling exponents were about 0.01, one fitted exponent was negative, and increasing context produced no monotonic trend.

relationships.reason: The size exponent varies about 4x with context length in Ranked and is near zero or negative in Binned, so it depends on objective, representation and context (r1–r10).
relationships.display_finding: The size exponent varied about fourfold with context length in Ranked and was near zero or negative in Binned.

relationships.reason: BIOscore generally rises as pre-training loss decreases (r11, r12; figure-only, stated by the authors).
relationships.display_finding: BIOscore generally improved as pretraining loss fell during training in both formulations.

relationships.condition: Across model size and between formulations
relationships.reason: Size gains are partly confounded by linear-probe capacity growing with width. Binned matches Ranked on BIOscore despite much weaker loss scaling (r11, r12).
relationships.display_finding: Binned matched Ranked on BIOscore despite much weaker loss scaling, while apparent model-size gains were partly confounded by linear-probe capacity increasing with width.
